## Overview

The Temuan people, also known as *Uwang/Eang Temuan* or *Orang Temuan*, are a Proto-Malay ethnic group indigenous to the western parts of Peninsular Malaysia. They live principally in rural and suburban villages in Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Melaka, and are also found in Johor and other states. Some Temuans live in urban settlements such as Desa Temuan on the outskirts of Petaling Jaya. They are classified by the Malaysian government as Orang Asli. Their language, Temuan, belongs to the Malay group of the Malayo-Polynesian languages within the Austronesian family and is closely related to Malay. Temuan folk culture combines forest-based subsistence, rice cultivation, village hierarchy, ancestor observances, animistic beliefs and ritual healing.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The sources mention that Temuans buy clothes, but provide no further information about their manufacture, styles or social use.

### Architecture

Temuan villages are generally located near the jungle, and Temuan communities traditionally lived in rural settlements. Nuclear families usually have their own houses, while the houses of close relatives are located nearby. The sources also describe government relocation to new villages and urban settlements. In Desa Temuan, on the outskirts of Petaling Jaya, residents rent out their homes to foreign workers.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do mention blowguns in a folk-history account, bamboo as a source of food preparation, and wood gathered from the jungle for construction.

## Music & performance

The Temuan sources describe music in connection with weddings and village celebrations. *Gogo*, also called *Bogeng* or *Bonggeng* in the sources, is village ceremonial dancing organized when Temuans marry. It takes place between 8 p.m. and 7 a.m. the following day. A live band plays music, and people from other villages join the dancing. The sources also state that younger Orang Asli, especially Temuans, are drawn to Bonggeng culture, in which young people at weddings are offered free food and remain awake all night with modern music.

The Temuan shaman leads the annual *sawai* or *sewang*, an earth-healing ritual held to honor ancestors and appease guardian spirits. Asyik FM, Malaysia’s national radio service, broadcasts daily in the Temuan language.

## Dance & theatre

*Gogo* or *Bogeng* is the named Temuan performance tradition in the sources. It is village ceremonial dancing associated with marriage celebrations. Weddings can bring together people from other villages, who dance throughout the night while a live band plays.

The sources also name *sawai* or *sewang*, led by a shaman as an ancient earth-healing ritual. This is described as a religious ceremony rather than theatrical entertainment.

## Festivals & rituals

The Temuan annual ritual calendar includes *sawai* or *sewang*, an earth-healing ceremony led by a shaman. During it, the Temuans honor their ancestors and seek to appease guardian spirits. The sources connect this ritual with traditional beliefs about nature spirits, illness and disasters.

The largest holiday in the Temuan community is *Aik Gayak Muyang*, also called *Aik Muyang* or Ancestor Day. It is held at the end of the year and the beginning of the new year, after the harvest and fruit picking. Different villages observe it on different dates, within a period from 15 December to 15 January. People gather for a feast and thank their God and ancestors for their crops and peaceful life. The sources list village dates including 29 December at Kampung Orang Asli Pulau Kempas, 30 December at Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Melut, Dengkil, 31 December at Kampung Orang Asli Bukit Tadom, Kampung Orang Asli Puchong and Kampung Putra, Jelebu, 1 January at Kampung Orang Asli Hulu Kuang, Rawang, 9 January at Kampung Orang Asli Bukit Machung, Hulu Selangor District, 10 January at Kampung Orang Asli Langkap Tanjung Ipoh, and 14 January at Kampung Orang Asli Serendah, Hulu Selangor District.

Marriage is associated with *Gogo* or *Bogeng*. The sources also describe customary observances concerning food, travel, storms, death and haunted places. A person who leaves a meal in a hurry without eating must *tempot*, touching the food to the skin, while a person traveling in light rain must put a leaf in the ear. Temuans are expected to remain quiet during thunderstorms, which they associate with the Thunder god hunting devils.

## Foodways

Rice is the main food crop. The sources name three varieties of wet rice: *masuri*, *pulut* and *malinja*. The crop is primarily used for household consumption, although many families still need to buy rice from stores because their fields do not produce enough. Temuan families also maintain backyard gardens where they grow vegetables and tropical fruits.

Jungle produce contributes both food and income. The sources name *durian*, *petai*, rattan and bamboo, and also mention wild fruits, medicinal plants and animals obtained through hunting. Temuans hunt wild boars, deer, monkeys, monitor lizards, porcupines and other animals and birds, and fish in surrounding rivers. Rubber and other commodity crops are grown for sale, with rubber providing much of the cash income.

Temuan food is usually cooked in bamboo. Named dishes include catfish *Tempoyak* cooked with *Semomok* leaf, *Ubi* with *Perah* fruit, *Lemang*, *Lepat* prepared with banana leaf, and *Ulam* with sambal. At *Aik Gayak Muyang*, people gather for a feast connected with thanking God and the ancestors for the harvest.

Traditional beliefs also shape food practices. During lunch or dinner, people throw some food to evil spirits through open doors or windows so that the spirits do not join the meal. Food bought or brought from outside is burned in the evening because of the perceived danger from spirits and ghosts.

## Oral tradition & literature

Temuan folk history tells of two brothers who took part in the gathering of earthly tribes during a time when people understood the language of animals. A storm overturned their ship. *Abang*, the older brother, saved his blowgun and reached the shore, while *Adik*, the younger brother, saved a sacred scroll. The story contrasts Abang’s continuation as a hunter-gatherer with Adik’s acquisition of knowledge, institutionalized religion and new laws.

Another origin story concerns the great flood. The sources say that many Temuans died after committing *Celau*, sins that angered God and the ancestors. Only *Mamak* and *Inak Bungsuk* survived by climbing an Eaglewood tree at *Gunung Raja*, also called *Gunung Rajah* or Royal Mountain, on the border of Selangor and Pahang. They survived because they possessed a mantra or spell that eased the storm. *Mamak Bungsuk* and *Inak Bungsuk* are described as Temuan analogues of Adam and Eve.

The sources state that the ancient history of Negeri Sembilan is preserved in oral traditions passed from generation to generation.

## Language & religion

Temuan is an Austronesian language in the Malay group of the Malayo-Polynesian languages. It is distinct from Malay but closely related to it and has mutual intelligibility with Malay. It is principally a spoken language with dialectal variation. The two major dialects are *Belandas* and *Mantra*. Examples given for Belandas include *diak* (“he/she”), *hajak* (“only”), *kitak* (“we”) and *tai*, an end-of-sentence particle. Mantra equivalents include *dien*, *hajen*, *kiten* and *tea*. Temuan is written in the Latin alphabet, although no standard orthography has been established; traditionally, the Temuan people had no written language.

The majority of Temuans follow traditional beliefs, while the sources give figures of 64.2% for traditional beliefs, 30% for Muslims and 5.8% for Christians. Traditional religion, *adat pepati*, is part of Temuan culture. The higher god is called *Tuhan*, while *Muyang* is identified as God. Temuans believe that they were placed on *Tanah Tujuh* to guard the rain forest. Their animism includes respect for guardian spirits associated with rivers, hills, streams, rocks, trees and shrubs. Shamans and folk healers, including the *dukun* and *bomoh*, use herbal remedies, trance and ritual ceremonies.
